title: Introduce WHO-recommended vaccines against childhood malaria

concept.text: Prevent clinical malaria in children through vaccines suitable for endemic-country immunization programmes. RTS,S and R21 achieved WHO recommendation, although neither completes the existing 90%-efficacy target. Proposed completion test: WHO recommendation for routine childhood use in endemic settings, based on clinical efficacy, safety and public-health benefit, followed by WHO prequalification for international procurement. Test set by: WHO, advised by SAGE and the Malaria Policy Advisory Group. Reported achieved: WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 on 6 October 2021 and R21/Matrix-M on 2 October 2023; both subsequently obtained WHO prequalification. Overlaps: INF-13. Sources given: [WHO RTS,S recommendation](https://www.who.int/News/Item/06-10-2021-Who-Recommends-Groundbreaking-Malaria-Vaccine-for-Children-at-Risk) ; [WHO R21 recommendation](https://www.who.int/news/item/02-10-2023-who-recommends-r21-matrix-m-vaccine-for-malaria-prevention-in-updated-advice-on-immunization) ; [WHO malaria vaccine questions and answers](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/q-a-on-rts-s-malaria-vaccine).

page.title: WHO-recommended childhood malaria vaccines
page.definition: Vaccines against Plasmodium falciparum, a malaria-causing parasite, are recommended by WHO for children in endemic areas and prequalified for procurement by United Nations agencies. RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M meet these conditions.

goal.need: WHO estimates that the African Region accounted for 95% of malaria deaths worldwide in 2024. Childhood immunization provides another route to malaria prevention: the 2019–2023 RTS,S implementation programme reached more than 2 million children in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi, and its evaluation attributed a 13% reduction in mortality to vaccination among children eligible by age.

figures.caption: WHO estimates of the malaria burden in 2024
figures.note: The childhood deaths are included in the worldwide death total.

statements.quote: The vaccine should reduce the incidence of all clinical malaria episodes.
statements.context: Preferred product characteristics for vaccines to reduce malaria morbidity and mortality.

statements.quote: Malaria vaccines should be provided as part of a comprehensive malaria control strategy.

completion.title: A WHO-recommended childhood malaria vaccine enters WHO’s List of Prequalified Vaccines.
completion.criterion: A vaccine recommended by WHO against childhood P. falciparum malaria is included in WHO’s List of Prequalified Vaccines following a positive evaluation of quality, safety, efficacy, manufacturing and suitability for the intended immunization programme. This procurement milestone was achieved by RTS,S/AS01 on 15 July 2022 and by R21/Matrix-M on 21 December 2023.
completion.set_by: WHO vaccine prequalification programme, List of Prequalified Vaccines.
completion.threshold_quote: meets WHO standard for vaccine quality, safety and efficacy standards, as endorsed by the WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization (ECBS)
completion.basis: WHO identifies prequalification as a prerequisite for UNICEF procurement and Gavi deployment support. It supplies the procurement test for a WHO-recommended vaccine. WHO’s separate preference for 90% efficacy against clinical malaria over 12 months is described as “highly preferred”; WHO explicitly recognizes the public-health potential of vaccines with lower efficacy.

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine reduces infection after human challenge at two-sided p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Reduce microscopy-detected P. falciparum infection versus unvaccinated controls after controlled human challenge, using the protocol’s two-sided 5% significance level and follow-up through day 28. The study published on 13 June 2016 found 26/30 adults protected with delayed fractional-dose RTS,S/AS01B versus 0/12 controls (p<0.0001). Its authors also recount the initial RTS,S/AS02 challenge result published in 1997: 6/7 adults protected. Adult challenge efficacy does not establish childhood field efficacy.
milestones.set_by: Regules et al., RTS,S/AS01 phase 2a protocol NCT01857869; this statistical test and follow-up period were specified for that study.
milestones.threshold_quote: All statistical tests were 2-tailed at 5% significance level.

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine reduces childhood clinical malaria with a 95% confidence interval above zero.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate positive efficacy against the prespecified clinical-malaria endpoint in a randomized phase 2 field trial, with the 95% confidence interval excluding zero. In the 2008 RTS,S/AS01E trial, 894 children aged 5–17 months were randomized in Kenya and Tanzania. Among 809 per-protocol participants, first clinical malaria occurred in 32/402 vaccine recipients and 66/407 controls: adjusted efficacy 53% (95% CI 28–69; p<0.001), over mean follow-up of 7.9 months. The endpoint required fever and more than 2500 parasites/µL.
milestones.set_by: Clinical efficacy convention applied by Bejon et al. in the randomized phase 2b trial NCT00380393; the quoted case definition is specific to that trial.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary end point was fever with a falciparum parasitemia density of more than 2500 parasites per microliter

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine reduces clinical-malaria episodes in a phase 3 trial at p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Show reduced clinical-malaria episodes in a randomized phase 3 trial at its specified significance level. The RTS,S final analysis used p<0.05: among 8922 children aged 5–17 months, four doses gave 36.3% efficacy (95% CI 31.8–40.5) over median follow-up of 48 months; the report’s issue date was 4 July 2015. R21’s phase 3 analysis included 4644 children aged 5–36 months: 12-month efficacy was 75% (95% CI 71–79) at seasonal sites and 68% (61–74) at standard sites, both p<0.0001; that report’s issue date was 10 February 2024.
milestones.set_by: RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, NCT00866619 final-analysis plan; the quoted significance threshold was specified for that analysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: p values less than 0·05 were deemed significant.

milestones.title: A childhood malaria vaccine receives a positive regulatory benefit–risk assessment.
milestones.criterion: Obtain a positive regulatory benefit–risk assessment of the vaccine’s quality, safety and efficacy for its intended childhood indication. EMA’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use issued a positive scientific opinion for Mosquirix (RTS,S/AS01) on 23 July 2015 under Article 58, for use outside the European Union. This scientific opinion is distinct from a national marketing authorization.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, Article 58 assessment of Mosquirix; this assessment route was used for RTS,S/AS01.
milestones.threshold_quote: The Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) therefore concluded that the benefits of the vaccine outweigh its risks

milestones.title: Routine childhood malaria vaccination resolves safety concerns and shows evidence of benefit.
milestones.criterion: Resolve concerns about meningitis, cerebral malaria and sex-specific mortality through exclusion of important risks or a positive benefit–risk assessment, and show severe-malaria or mortality trends consistent with benefit. In 158 randomized clusters in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi, 652673 children had received at least one RTS,S dose by 30 April 2021. No excess of the specified safety outcomes was detected; severe-malaria hospital admissions fell 32% (95% CI 5–51) among children eligible for three doses. These interim results informed WHO’s recommendation.
milestones.set_by: WHO SAGE and Malaria Policy Advisory Committee, 2019 framework for policy decision on RTS,S/AS01; this pilot requirement was written for RTS,S/AS01.
milestones.threshold_quote: concerns regarding the safety signals observed in the Phase 3 trial (related to meningitis, cerebral malaria and sex-specific mortality) are satisfactorily resolved

milestones.title: WHO recommends a malaria vaccine for childhood use in endemic areas.
milestones.criterion: WHO recommends the vaccine to prevent P. falciparum malaria in children in endemic areas, prioritizing moderate and high transmission, within comprehensive malaria control. The current schedule comprises four doses from around 5 months of age. WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 on 6 October 2021 and R21/Matrix-M on 2 October 2023.
milestones.set_by: WHO, following advice from SAGE and the Malaria Policy Advisory Group; the quoted schedule is from its 2021 RTS,S/AS01 recommendation.
milestones.threshold_quote: RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine should be provided in a schedule of 4 doses in children from 5 months of age

results.finding: Delayed fractional-dose RTS,S/AS01B protected 26 of 30 adults after challenge, versus 0 of 12 controls.
results.detail: Blood-slide detection was followed through day 28. The two-sided Fisher exact test gave p<0.0001. This adult challenge result does not establish childhood field efficacy.

results.finding: RTS,S/AS01E in 809 children: adjusted efficacy against clinical malaria was 53% (95% CI, 28–69%).
results.detail: The randomized field trial used fever with more than 2,500 P. falciparum parasites per microliter as its primary endpoint. Mean follow-up was 7.9 months.
results.quote:
the adjusted efficacy rate for RTS,S/AS01E was 53% (95% 
confidence interval [CI], 28 to 69; P<0.001) on the basis of Cox regression.

results.finding: R21/Matrix-M in 293 children: 74% efficacy against clinical malaria (95% CI 63–82) at 6 months.
results.detail: In the randomized phase 2b field trial, 146 children received R21 with the lower Matrix-M dose and 147 received the control vaccine. The prespecified primary endpoint required fever and more than 5,000 P. falciparum parasites/µL.
results.quote: A Cox regression model comparing group 1 with group 3 resulted in vaccine efficacy of 74% (95% CI 63–82; p<0·0001).

results.finding: RTS,S/AS01 achieved 36.3% efficacy against clinical malaria in 8,922 children aged 5–17 months.
results.detail: In the randomized phase 3 trial, the four-dose group was compared with controls over a median 48 months of follow-up. Table 1 reports p<0.0001.
results.quote:
compared with 9585 episodes of
clinical malaria that met the primary case definition in children in the C3C
group, 6616 episodes occurred in the R3R group (VE 36·3%, 95% CI
31·8–40·5)

results.finding: R21/Matrix-M in 4,644 children: 75% efficacy against multiple clinical-malaria episodes at seasonal sites (p<0.0001).
results.detail: Randomized, double-blind phase 3 trial; modified per-protocol analysis over 12 months after the primary vaccination series. Efficacy against multiple episodes was 67% at standard sites (p<0.0001).
results.quote: Similarly, vaccine efficacy against multiple clinical malaria episodes was 75% (71–78; p<0·0001) at the seasonal sites and 67% (59–73; p<0·0001) at standard sites.

results.finding: Mosquirix: CHMP issued a positive benefit–risk opinion on 23 July 2015; the supporting study involved over 12,000 children.
results.detail: The opinion covers immunisation of children aged 6 weeks to 17 months for use outside the EU; it is distinct from national marketing authorization.
results.quote: The Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) therefore concluded that the benefits of the vaccine outweigh its risks and issued a positive scientific opinion.

results.finding: In 158 randomized clusters, 652,673 children received at least one RTS,S dose; severe-malaria admissions fell 32% among children eligible for three doses.
results.detail: No excess of the specified safety outcomes was detected, and the findings informed WHO's recommendation. Cerebral malaria estimates had wide confidence intervals and did not exclude the diluted effect seen in the earlier trial.
results.quote: Among children eligible for three vaccine doses, RTS,S introduction was associated with a 32% reduction (95% CI 5–51%) in hospital admission with severe malaria, and a 9% reduction (95% CI 0–18%) in all-cause mortality (excluding injury).

results.finding: In 158 randomized clusters, RTS,S introduction was associated with a mortality rate ratio of 0.87 among children eligible for three doses.
results.detail: Updated surveillance found no excess risk of cerebral malaria or meningitis. Mortality rate ratios were 0.85 for girls and 0.87 for boys; their ratio was 1.00 (95% CI 0.90–1.12).
results.quote: The mortality rate ratio was 0·87 (95% CI 0·77–0·97; p=0·016).

results.finding: WHO recommends RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M for children in malaria-endemic areas on a 4-dose schedule.
results.detail: The recommendation prioritizes moderate and high transmission areas, includes comprehensive malaria control, and starts vaccination from 5 months of age. No sample size applies.
results.quote:
WHO recommends the use of malaria vaccines for the prevention of P. falciparum malaria in 
children living in malaria endemic areas, prioritizing areas of moderate and high transmission.

results.finding: Mosquirix malaria vaccine: WHO prequalification effective 15 July 2022; sample size not applicable.
R21/Matrix-M childhood malaria vaccine was added to WHO’s prequalified vaccines list on 21 December 2023; sample size not applicable.
results.detail: WHO had recommended R21/Matrix-M for malaria prevention in children. Its prequalification process evaluates safety, efficacy, manufacturing standards and suitability for immunization programmes.
results.quote: The R21 vaccine is the second malaria vaccine prequalified by WHO, following the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine which obtained prequalification status in July 2022.
